title: How a Jataka works
hookLine: each tale has a present story, a past story, and a last line saying who each character was

lines: A FABLE ABOUT SOMEONE THEY KNEW.
cards: The talkative tortoise was Kokalika. The wise minister was the Bodhisatta. That's how one tale ends, in the Jataka, the great collection of stories about the Buddha's past lives.
Two sentences, and suddenly a fable about a tortoise is also about a monk the listeners knew. Before the longer tales of the coming weeks, today is about the frame they share.
Learn the frame once, and the tales that follow get easier to read.

teach.b: First, a story in the present. A tale opens in the Buddha's own lifetime, with something that has just happened among the monks.

In the tortoise tale, a monk named Kokalika has come to ruin through his own careless tongue, and the monks are talking about it. The Buddha says: this isn't the first time his tongue has brought him down.
Second, a story in the past. Long ago, when a king reigned in Benares, the Bodhisatta, the Buddha in an earlier life, was that king's minister. The king talked without stopping.
Meanwhile, a tortoise made friends with two young geese, and they offered to fly him home with them, if he'd bite the middle of a stick and keep his mouth shut. Up they went.
Villagers below shouted and laughed at the sight. The tortoise opened his mouth to answer back, let go of the stick, and fell into the king's courtyard.

The minister used the broken tortoise to teach the king to talk less. Third, the verses. Somewhere in the tale, someone speaks a short verse, here the Bodhisatta to his king, the lesson pressed into a few lines.
Fourth, who was who. Then the Buddha connects the two stories. The tortoise was Kokalika.

teach.h: THE LAST LINE IS THE HINGE.
teach.b: That last line is the hinge.
It turns an old fable into a mirror: the same habits, the same people, coming round again. When you read a Jataka, you can start at the end. The last line tells you who to watch.

how: Jataka tales are retold, painted and performed in Theravada communities, and in the collection each tale closes by saying who each character was.

o: the closing link: the Buddha says who was who
the short verse that holds a tale's lesson
the opening story set in the Buddha's lifetime

games.q: how a Jataka works: tap the pairs.
p: something just happened among the monks
a tale from a former life

s: a Jataka tale begins in the distant past
it begins in the Buddha's own lifetime, with something that has just happened, then goes back.
the last line connects the past characters to people in the present
in the tortoise tale: the tortoise was Kokalika, the wise minister was the Bodhisatta.
the Bodhisatta is always the hero who wins the day
in the tortoise tale he's the minister who teaches from what happened, not the one who flies.

games.q: you're the tortoise, flying high, biting a stick carried by two geese. villagers below are laughing at you. what do you do?
o: keep your mouth shut and enjoy the view.
open your mouth to answer them back.
close your eyes and wait to land.
games.why: he opens his mouth to answer back, lets go of the stick, and falls into the king's courtyard. the minister makes a lesson of it.

practice: Hold the tortoise tale's last line: the tortoise was Kokalika; the wise minister was the Bodhisatta.

Then bring up one small moment from your week, a conversation, a mistake, a kindness, tell it as a tiny fable in your mind, and give it a last line: who was the tortoise there, and who was the wise minister?
You might be both, so just see who was who, without judging.

wordCard.voice: Samodhana. The connection: the closing part of a Jataka where the Buddha says who was who, after a story in the present and a story in the past. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali samodhana: the connection, the closing part of a Jataka, where the Buddha says who was who.
